Grade 1

Sky Patterns

What patterns do we see in the sky, and how can we predict them? (Predict means to guess what will happen next.)

The sky follows patterns we can watch and predict. This unit covers why day and night repeat, how the Moon seems to change shape, why stars are still there in the daytime, and how the amount of daylight in Michigan changes with the seasons.

In this lesson

  1. Day and night repeat
  2. The Moon and stars have patterns
  3. Seasons change the amount of daylight
  4. Try it at home
  5. Check yourself
  6. Sky pattern line

You did this before / what is new. This is new in grade 1: day and night, Moon shapes, and a daylight strip log by season. Weather watching in kindergarten helps you keep a calendar.

Concept 1

Day and night repeat

Earth spins all the time. As it spins, your place turns to face the Sun, and that is day. Later your place turns away from the Sun, and that is night.

Try it

Use a lamp and ball. Turn the ball slowly.

Safety: An adult sets up the lamp. Use an LED lamp if you can.

“Where is the light? Where is it dark?”

Data

Guess first: What will you see in the sky in the daytime, and what at night?

What you need:

  • Two sheets of paper
  • Crayons

Do: Fold a paper in half. On one side draw the day sky: the Sun, clouds, blue. On the other side draw the night sky: dark, the Moon, stars. Use the example below to check your drawing.

Look for: Which things are only in the day sky? Which are only in the night sky?

What it shows: The sky has a pattern: Sun in the day, Moon and stars at night.

“Sun in day. Stars at night.”

Real world

In Michigan, noon is bright and midnight is dark.

“Noon: light. Midnight: dark.”

Concept 2

The Moon and stars have patterns

The Moon’s shape seems to change, and stars are visible at night but not in the bright daytime sky.

Diagram

Moon with sunlight arrows.

“The Moon does not make its own light.”

Reflect means to bounce light back, like a mirror. The Moon does not make its own light. It reflects sunlight.

Try it

A Moon phase is the shape of the Moon we see.

What you do:

  • Put the Moon-phase cards in order: thin crescent, half, round.
  • Say what changes from one card to the next.

“The Moon’s shape seems to change over time.”

Data

Class Moon calendar.

Guess first: Will the Moon look the same every night?

What you need:

  • A sheet of paper
  • Crayons, or the four Moon pictures on this page

Do: Look at the Moon on a clear night once a week for four weeks. Draw the shape you see. If the sky is cloudy, use the four pictures.

Look for: Does the shape change from week to week? Does it come back to the same shape?

What it shows: The Moon’s shape changes and then repeats about every month.

“The Moon looked different after 2 weeks.”

Real world

Stars are faraway suns. They are still there in the daytime, but the bright sky hides them.

A galaxy is a huge group of stars. Some faint smudges of light in the night sky are galaxies, so far away they look like soft clouds of light.

“Stars are faraway suns. Some faint lights are whole galaxies.”

Concept 3

Seasons change the amount of daylight

In Michigan, summer days have more daylight and winter days have less daylight.

Data

Paper-strip daylight graph: long strip for summer, short strip for winter.

Guess first: Which month has the most squares of light: December, March, or June?

What you need:

  • The daylight bar graph on this page
  • A pencil and two crayons

Do: Look at the bar graph and count the squares for each month. On a copy of the graph (or a blank grid), color one square for each hour of daylight. June gets about 15 colored squares, March about 12, and December about 9.

Look for: Which month has the longest colored row? Which has the shortest?

What it shows: The longest row is June. More daylight comes in summer.

“Count the squares. More squares means more daylight.”

Try it

Guess first: In which month is the Sun up longer in Michigan, June or December?

What you need:

  • Two pictures of the same Michigan place, one in June and one in December
  • Or paper strips and a ruler marked in inches and centimeters

Do: Look at the two pictures. Where is the Sun? Is it light or dark? Next, cut a long strip for June and a short strip for December (the page’s graph shows about 15 and 9 squares of daylight).

Look for: In June it is light late in the evening. In December it gets dark early.

What it shows: Summer days have more daylight than winter days.

“June: light late. December: dark early.”

Real world

In Michigan the Sun is up for more hours in summer and fewer hours in winter.

Try this: Ask a grown-up for the sunset time in your town on a June day and on a December day. Compare them. The June sunset is much later.

“Summer: the Sun is up a long time. Winter: not so long.”

Real world

Michigan summer evenings stay light late. On a summer evening you can play outside after dinner, and the sky stays light for a long time. In winter, it can already be dark at dinner time. A beach or park near the Great Lakes is a good place to notice this.

“Summer light stays late.”

Hands-on · Design or investigate

Try it at home or in class

Paper-plate sundial. A sundial is a clock that uses the shadow of the Sun. Students build a simple sundial with a paper plate, straw, and tape. On a sunny day, they mark the shadow at morning, noon, and afternoon. Criteria: the shadow marks change in a predictable way. If the sky is cloudy, use provided shadow-position cards to complete the pattern. This supports observation of predictable sky patterns.

Try it

What you need

  • Ball
  • Lamp or strong flashlight
  • Paper plates
  • Straw
  • Tape
  • Crayons
  • Moon-phase cards
  • Paper strips
  • Provided data cards

Safety: Adult handles anything warm, such as a lamp that gets hot. Use an LED lamp if possible. Use a ready-made flashlight or LED lamp; do not open the battery compartment.

Try it

What you do

1. Lamp and ball (10 minutes). Turn the ball slowly in front of the lamp. Which side is lit (day)? Which is dark (night)?

2. Moon cards (10 minutes). Put the Moon-phase cards in order: crescent, half, round.

3. Daylight strips (10 minutes). Make a long strip for June and a short strip for December.

4. Sundial (30 minutes, sunny day). Mark the straw’s shadow in the morning, at noon, and in the afternoon. Notice that the shadow moves.

No time or no good weather? Use this data

This data is a backup. It lets you practice reading evidence, but your own observations are better when you can collect them.

  • Real observation log: Begin a daylight strip log in fall. Each week, mark about how long it is light. You may also draw Moon shapes when they are visible.
  • Provided dataset: Daylight strips for southern Michigan: December about 9 squares, March about 12 squares, June about 15 squares (each square is about one hour of daylight).
  • Moon-phase card sequence and day/night star visibility cards.

Use the provided dataset if weather, school schedule, or cloudy days prevent real observations. With the backup, you do not observe the sky yourself: you graph the three months as strips and say that more daylight comes with summer.

Near you: Michigan summer evenings stay light late; winter afternoons get dark early. On a clear night by Lake Michigan or Lake Huron, the Moon can make a bright path of light on the water. Michigan has dark-sky parks for star watching. Child text: “In Michigan, summer evenings stay light late. Winter evenings get dark early.”

Words to know

Sky
Where we see the Sun, Moon, clouds, and stars.
Pattern
Something that repeats.
Rotate
To spin.
Horizon
The line where sky meets land.
Daylight
The time when the Sun is up.
Season
A time of year, like winter or summer.
Moon phase
The shape of the Moon we see.
Star
A faraway sun.
Galaxy
A huge group of stars, so far away it looks like a soft cloud of light.
Reflect
To bounce light back, like a mirror.
Sundial
A clock that uses the shadow of the Sun.
Predict
To say what may happen next.
Tutor notes: misconceptions and pacing

Pacing: 5 sessions of 30 minutes.

Common misconceptions to listen for:

  • “The Sun goes around Earth.” Correct: Earth rotates; the Sun appears to move across the sky.
  • “The Sun turns off at night.” Correct: the Sun shines; our part of Earth turns away.
  • “The Moon makes its own light.” Correct: the Moon reflects sunlight.
  • “The Moon is a lamp, fire, or star.” Correct: the Moon does not make its own visible light.
  • “Stars disappear during the day.” Correct: stars are still there, but the bright sky hides them.
  • “Stars turn off in daytime.” Correct: they remain in the sky, but we cannot see them in daylight.
  • “Summer happens because Earth is closer to the Sun.” Correct: Earth is not closer in summer. Day length changes with the seasons; the reason comes in later grades.
  • “Day length is the same everywhere and every season.” Correct: day length changes with season and place.

Limits and cautions:

  • Sky observations need clear days. The full path is the student’s own log; if observations cannot happen, the provided data are a partial path (analysis of provided data), not observations.
  • The daylight strip log should start in fall if possible; if the unit is taught in spring, use the provided dataset.
  • Moon phases do not require nightly observation; cards or short videos are acceptable.
  • The tilt explanation is simplified; do not say Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.
  • This unit does not teach Moon-phase causes in depth, constellation names, or planetary orbits. Those belong in later grades.

What the unit covers: The cards and provided data cover describing patterns of the Sun, Moon, and stars, and graphing daylight data. Full coverage needs the child’s own observations: a Moon drawing on clear nights and a daylight strip log kept over the year.

Connections:

  • Builds on: Noticing and Asking (optional); Sunlight, Weather, and Staying Safe, for sunlight and seasonal observations.
  • Builds toward: Earth in Space; Where We’re Going; Gravity, Orbits & the Solar System.

After the lesson · Activity

Sky pattern line

Build the day and night pattern with paper cards. No screen needed.

Try it

What you need:

  • Six paper cards: Sun (day), Moon (night), stars (night), a thin crescent Moon, a half Moon, a round Moon
  • Tape, or a table to lay them out on

Do: Lay the day and night cards in a line. Put the Sun card first, then the Moon and stars cards, then the Sun card again. Say what repeats.

Then: Put the three Moon-shape cards in order from thin crescent to round. Say what you notice.

“You built a pattern: day, then night, then day again.”
